AI & automation: Gigs built around AI tools and automation software: setting up chatbots and automated workflows for businesses, selling AI-made products, or offering services that AI speeds up. Most cost little to start, but the tools change quickly and many creators overstate how hands-off these businesses really are.
Local & professional services: Service businesses you run from a home office for local clients or professionals: bookkeeping, lead generation, virtual assistance, marketing for local businesses, and similar work. Income depends on finding and keeping clients, so selling matters as much as the service itself.
E-commerce: Selling physical or print-on-demand goods online through Etsy, Amazon, Shopify and similar stores, including dropshipping and reselling. Startup costs are usually low, but margins, platform fees and competition decide whether the numbers work.
Marketing & content: Getting paid to promote other people's products or businesses: affiliate marketing, ad management, social media management, copywriting and similar work. Some of it pays per job and some per sale, and results usually depend on building an audience or a client list first.
Physical & print products: Making things at home to sell: crafts, printed goods, candles, embroidery, 3D prints and other small-batch products. These usually need some equipment and space, and the time it takes to make each item limits how far they can grow.
Digital & subscription products: Products you make once and sell many times: printables, templates, courses, e-books, stock assets and paid memberships. Each sale costs almost nothing to fill, but the marketplaces are crowded, so the hard part is getting found.
Content & personal brand: Earning from your own audience on YouTube, TikTok, podcasts, newsletters or blogs, through ads, sponsorships and your own products. This is the slowest category to pay off, and most people in it earn little until they have built a sizable following.
